content: The Care for Infants and Young Children: Implementation Review and Planning Guide is part of the Primary Health Care Quality Improvement Guide, specifically Module 3, which focuses on improving services for infants and young children. Published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2024, this guide provides a structured approach to assess and enhance the quality of primary health care for children under the age of three, who are at the highest risk of illness and death. It emphasizes both survive interventions, such as vaccination, management of childhood illnesses, and nutrition, and thrive interventions, which include early childhood development, prevention of injuries, and addressing abuse and neglect. The guide outlines a methodology for continuous monitoring and periodic evaluations of child health services at primary care facilities, such as health centers, posts, and outpatient hospital departments. It includes tools like checklists to assess clinical care, policies, supplies, and the environment. These tools help identify areas needing improvement and develop actionable plans for individual facilities. External teams can also use the same checklists to evaluate services across multiple facilities at district, provincial, or national levels, synthesizing findings to inform broader planning. The guide highlights the importance of engaging local health staff in identifying and solving problems through bottom-up planning. By collecting and monitoring facility data, progress can be tracked and continuously improved. It also stresses the need for frontline health workers to be adequately trained and supported to provide essential services, including managing sick children, screening for preventable conditions, and offering counseling and family support. Key interventions for infants and young children include exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, complementary feeding starting at six months, growth monitoring, management of malnutrition, routine immunizations, and prevention and treatment of common childhood illnesses like pneumonia, diarrhea, and malaria. The guide also addresses screening and management of developmental delays, disabilities, and signs of abuse, as well as promoting early childhood education and injury prevention. The guide provides detailed instructions for conducting facility reviews, including interviews with caregivers to assess the effectiveness of health services. Caregivers are asked about breastfeeding practices, complementary feeding, and their understanding of danger signs that require immediate medical attention. Health workers are evaluated on their ability to provide appropriate advice and counseling on these topics. The WHO emphasizes that improving child health services contributes to achieving broader Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as reducing poverty and hunger, improving education, ensuring gender equality, and providing access to clean water and sanitation.
